claim: Fowler describes a circuit breaker as a wrapper that, once failures reach a threshold, trips and returns errors without making the protected call.
quote: Once the failures reach a certain threshold, the circuit breaker trips, and all further calls to the circuit breaker return with an error, without the protected call being made at all.

claim: Fowler adds a half-open state in which the breaker makes a trial call to see if the problem is fixed.
quote: There is now a third state present - half open - meaning the circuit is ready to make a real call as trial to see if the problem is fixed.
note: The hyphens around 'half open' are plain hyphen-minus in the source.

claim: In the half-open state a successful trial call resets the breaker; a failed one restarts the timeout.
quote: Asked to call in the half-open state results in a trial call, which will either reset the breaker if successful or restart the timeout if not.

claim: Fowler credits Michael Nygard's book Release It with popularizing the Circuit Breaker pattern.
quote: Michael Nygard popularized the Circuit Breaker pattern to prevent this kind of catastrophic cascade.
note: Preceding words in source: 'In his excellent book Release It,' (the link text reads 'Release It' without the exclamation mark).

claim: Release It! Second Edition by Michael Nygard was published by the Pragmatic Bookshelf in January 2018, with Circuit Breaker and Bulkheads among its stability patterns.
quote: Stability Patterns Timeouts Circuit Breaker Bulkheads Steady State Fail Fast Let It Crash Handshaking Test Harnesses Decoupling Middleware Shed Load Create Back Pressure Governor
source: Pragmatic Bookshelf, Release It! Second Edition (book page, table of contents)
note: Page lists 'Published: January 2018'. The first edition was 2007 per common knowledge, but the page only says 'the best-selling first edition of this book' with no date; first-edition date not verified here.

claim: Netflix Hystrix is no longer in active development and is in maintenance mode.
quote: Hystrix is no longer in active development, and is currently in maintenance mode.
note: Date is the README commit a7df971cba (2018-11-19) that added the maintenance notice, per the GitHub commits API. Last stable version named in README: 1.5.18.

claim: Netflix recommends resilience4j for new projects instead of Hystrix.
quote: we intend to continue using Hystrix for existing applications, and to leverage open and active projects like resilience4j for new internal projects. We are beginning to recommend others do the same.
note: Markdown link syntax around 'resilience4j' removed.

claim: Netflix shifted focus from Hystrix's preconfigured settings toward adaptive implementations such as adaptive concurrency limits.
quote: our focus has shifted towards more adaptive implementations that react to an application's real time performance rather than pre-configured settings
note: Source uses a curly apostrophe in application's.

claim: Hystrix circuitBreaker.requestVolumeThreshold defaults to 20 requests in the rolling window before the circuit can trip.
quote: For example, if the value is 20, then if only 19 requests are received in the rolling window (say a window of 10 seconds) the circuit will not trip open even if all 19 failed.
note: Default Value table cell for circuitBreaker.requestVolumeThreshold reads 20.

claim: Hystrix circuitBreaker.errorThresholdPercentage defaults to 50 percent.
quote: This property sets the error percentage at or above which the circuit should trip open and start short-circuiting requests to fallback logic.
note: Default Value table cell reads 50.

claim: Hystrix circuitBreaker.sleepWindowInMilliseconds defaults to 5000 ms.
quote: This property sets the amount of time, after tripping the circuit, to reject requests before allowing attempts again to determine if the circuit should again be closed.
note: Default Value table cell reads 5000.

claim: Hystrix execution.isolation.thread.timeoutInMilliseconds defaults to 1000 ms.
quote: This property sets the time in milliseconds after which the caller will observe a timeout and walk away from the command execution.
note: Default Value table cell reads 1000.

claim: Hystrix metrics.rollingStats.timeInMilliseconds defaults to 10000 ms (10 s).
quote: This property sets the duration of the statistical rolling window, in milliseconds. This is how long Hystrix keeps metrics for the circuit breaker to use and for publishing.
note: Default Value table cell reads 10000.

claim: resilience4j's CircuitBreaker is a finite state machine with CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN and special states METRICS_ONLY, DISABLED and FORCED_OPEN.
quote: The CircuitBreaker is implemented via a finite state machine with three normal states: CLOSED, OPEN and HALF_OPEN and three special states METRICS_ONLY, DISABLED and FORCED_OPEN.

claim: After the wait duration, resilience4j moves from OPEN to HALF_OPEN and permits a configurable number of trial calls.
quote: After a wait time duration has elapsed, the CircuitBreaker state changes from OPEN to HALF_OPEN and permits a configurable number of calls to see if the backend is still unavailable or has become available again.

claim: In resilience4j v2.4.0 source, default failure rate threshold is 50%, slow call rate threshold 100%, and wait duration in open state 60 s.
quote: public static final int DEFAULT_FAILURE_RATE_THRESHOLD = 50; // Percentage public static final int DEFAULT_SLOW_CALL_RATE_THRESHOLD = 100; // Percentage public static final int DEFAULT_WAIT_DURATION_IN_OPEN_STATE = 60; // Seconds

claim: In resilience4j v2.4.0 source, defaults are 10 permitted calls in half-open, minimum 100 calls, sliding window size 100, slow call threshold 60 s, COUNT_BASED window.
quote: public static final int DEFAULT_PERMITTED_CALLS_IN_HALF_OPEN_STATE = 10; public static final int DEFAULT_MINIMUM_NUMBER_OF_CALLS = 100; public static final int DEFAULT_SLIDING_WINDOW_SIZE = 100; public static final int DEFAULT_SLOW_CALL_DURATION_THRESHOLD = 60; // Seconds
note: Same file: DEFAULT_SLIDING_WINDOW_TYPE = SlidingWindowType.COUNT_BASED. Docs table agrees: failureRateThreshold 50, slowCallRateThreshold 100, slowCallDurationThreshold 60000 ms, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState 10, slidingWindowType COUNT_BASED, slidingWindowSize 100, minimumNumberOfCalls 100, waitDurationInOpenState 60000 ms.

claim: resilience4j needs minimumNumberOfCalls recorded before computing a failure rate.
quote: Configures the minimum number of calls which are required (per sliding window period) before the CircuitBreaker can calculate the error rate or slow call rate.

claim: Envoy circuit breaking is enforced at the network level and is fully distributed, not coordinated, with limits per upstream cluster and priority.
quote: Envoy supports various types of fully distributed (not coordinated) circuit breaking:
source: Envoy docs, Architecture overview: Circuit breaking (1.40.0-dev-e07c88)
note: Same page: 'Each circuit breaking limit is configurable and tracked on a per upstream cluster and per priority basis.' Envoy has no per-host closed/open/half-open state machine here; limits are thresholds on connections, pending requests, requests and retries.

claim: Envoy enforces circuit breaking in the proxy rather than in each application.
quote: One of the main benefits of an Envoy mesh is that Envoy enforces circuit breaking limits at the network level as opposed to having to configure and code each application independently.
source: Envoy docs, Architecture overview: Circuit breaking (1.40.0-dev-e07c88)

claim: Envoy circuit breakers are on by default with modest values such as 1024 connections per cluster.
quote: Circuit breakers are enabled by default and have modest default values, e.g. 1024 connections per cluster.
source: Envoy docs, Architecture overview: Circuit breaking (1.40.0-dev-e07c88)

claim: Envoy circuit breaker threshold max_connections defaults to 1024.
quote: The maximum number of connections that Envoy will make to the upstream cluster. If not specified, the default is 1024.

claim: Envoy circuit breaker threshold max_pending_requests defaults to 1024.
quote: The maximum number of pending requests that Envoy will allow to the upstream cluster. If not specified, the default is 1024.

claim: Envoy circuit breaker threshold max_requests defaults to 1024.
quote: The maximum number of parallel requests that Envoy will make to the upstream cluster. If not specified, the default is 1024.

claim: Envoy circuit breaker threshold max_retries defaults to 3.
quote: The maximum number of parallel retries that Envoy will allow to the upstream cluster. If not specified, the default is 3.

claim: Envoy outlier detection consecutive_5xx defaults to 5.
quote: The number of consecutive server-side error responses (for HTTP traffic, 5xx responses; for TCP traffic, connection failures; for Redis, failure to respond PONG; etc.) before a consecutive 5xx ejection occurs. Defaults to 5.

claim: Envoy outlier detection interval defaults to 10 s.
quote: The time interval between ejection analysis sweeps. This can result in both new ejections as well as hosts being returned to service. Defaults to 10000ms or 10s.

claim: Envoy outlier detection base_ejection_time defaults to 30 s and is multiplied by the number of times the host has been ejected.
quote: The real time is equal to the base time multiplied by the number of times the host has been ejected and is capped by max_ejection_time . Defaults to 30000ms or 30s.
note: Spaces before '.' come from the docs' inline code markup as rendered to text.

claim: Envoy outlier detection max_ejection_percent defaults to 10%.
quote: The maximum % of an upstream cluster that can be ejected due to outlier detection. Defaults to 10% .
note: Spaces before '.' come from the docs' inline code markup as rendered to text.

claim: Stripe runs four kinds of limiters in production.
quote: At Stripe, we operate 4 different types of limiters in production.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters

claim: Stripe's request rate limiter restricts each user to N requests per second and is the most important limiter.
quote: The first one, the Request Rate Limiter , is by far the most important one.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters
note: Section text: 'This rate limiter restricts each user to N requests per second.'

claim: Stripe's concurrent requests limiter caps requests in progress at the same time.
quote: Instead of “You can use our API 1000 times a second”, this rate limiter says “You can only have 20 API requests in progress at the same time”.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters

claim: Stripe's fleet usage load shedder reserves a fraction (e.g. 20%) of infrastructure for critical requests and rejects excess non-critical ones with 503.
quote: We always reserve a fraction of our infrastructure for critical requests. If our reservation number is 20%, then any non-critical request over their 80% allocation would be rejected with status code 503.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters

claim: Stripe's worker utilization load shedder is the final line of defense, shedding lower-priority traffic when workers back up.
quote: This load shedder is the final line of defense. If your workers start getting backed up with requests, then this will shed lower-priority traffic.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters
note: Traffic categories, in source order: Critical methods, POSTs, GETs, Test mode traffic; test mode traffic is shed first.

claim: Stripe distinguishes load shedders, which decide on whole-system state, from per-user rate limiters.
quote: A load shedder makes its decisions based on the whole state of the system rather than the user who is making the request.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters

claim: Stripe implements rate limiting with a token bucket per user, stored in Redis.
quote: We use the token bucket algorithm to do rate limiting. This algorithm has a centralized bucket host where you take tokens on each request, and slowly drip more tokens into the bucket.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters
note: Same section: 'every Stripe user has a bucket' and 'We implement our rate limiters using Redis.'

claim: Stripe advises kill switches to disable rate limiters that kick in erroneously.
quote: Make sure you have kill switches to disable the rate limiters should they kick in erroneously.
source: Stripe blog, Paul Tarjan, Scaling your API with rate limiters

claim: Cloudflare approximates a sliding window by weighting the previous fixed window's count by the fraction of it still in the window.
source: Cloudflare blog, Julien Desgats, How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains
note: Example: 18 requests in the current minute that started 15 s ago, 42 in the previous minute.

claim: The approximation assumes a constant request rate during the previous window.
quote: This algorithm assumes a constant rate of requests during the previous sampling period (which can be any time span), this is why the result is only an approximation of the actual rate.
source: Cloudflare blog, Julien Desgats, How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains

claim: On 400 million requests, 0.003% were wrongly allowed or rate limited, with an average 6% difference between real and approximate rate.
quote: an analysis on 400 million requests from 270,000 distinct sources shown: 0.003% of requests have been wrongly allowed or rate limited An average difference of 6% between real rate and the approximate rate
source: Cloudflare blog, Julien Desgats, How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains
note: List items run together in extracted text; 'shown' is the source's wording. Also: no false positives, 3 false negatives each under 15% above threshold.
